the developmental neurotoxicity in the rat brain is observed after perinatal (in utero and lactation) exposure to a re-constructed chemical mixture of persistent organics, which mimics the blood profile of people living in Great Lake Basin.
in utero exposure to a mixture of persistent organics leads to significant transcriptional changes in the cholinergic and structural genes in the brain of adult female rats.

perinatal exposure of the rat to a reconstituited mixture of persistent organo-chlorine pollutants (PCBs, DDE, DDT, HCB, and HCHs) resulted in changes in the expression of genes involved in cholinergic and neurofilament signaling in the adult rat brain, and that these changes are associated with a decrease in the number of neurons in the subventricle zone of the brain.

the developmental neurobiology of the brain and the potential for adverse developmental outcomes in the brain following exposure to environmental toxicants, such as POPs, during early stages of brain development.
the effects of environmental mixtures of POPs on the developing brain and how this might affect behavior and learning.
the developmental neuropathological effects of environmentally relevant levels of POPs.

exposure to environmentally relevant mixtures of POPs during critical developmental periods can lead to significant neurodevelopmental changes in the brain.

a mixture of environmentally relevant POPs can lead to developmental changes that can be detected in the adult brain.
a mixture of environmental pollutants can lead to changes in the adult brain, even when no changes are detected at earlier developmental stages.
